mainTopic: Meat that went out of sight (בשר שנתעלם מן העין): רב's strict view, signs and omens, and identifying lost items by סימן or טביעות עין
overview: The amud opens by finishing a story about a man who lost one animal head in the river and pulled up two. רב forbade both, explaining that forbidden meat was more common there. The גמרא notes that this happened at a gentile port, so the case may not teach a rule for everywhere. It then asks how רב ever ate meat, and answers that he ate it right away, tied and sealed, or marked with a סימן. A story about רב, a ferry and a meal at his son-in-law's house leads into a discussion of signs: נחש versus סימן, the signs used by רב, שמואל and רבי יוחנן, and the story of שמואל and רבי יוחנן's letters. The גמרא then returns to meat that went out of sight. Strung pieces count as a סימן, and meat dropped by ravens on ערב יום כיפור is permitted because kosher meat is more common that day. Three stories show that טביעות עין, recognizing an item by sight, is also enough. The amud ends as רבא begins to explain how he changed his mind about whether a סימן or טביעות עין is stronger, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The man who lost one head and found two
steps.stepSummary: A man dropped an animal's head into the river, pulled out two heads with a basket, and רב forbade both of them to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He was cleaning an animal's head, and it fell from him. He went and brought a basket, threw it in, and brought up two. רב said: Does it really happen like that? He forbade them to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a story about a man who lost one head in the river and found two, and רב forbade both.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since he lost one and found two, at least one head is clearly not his. So רב reasons that maybe neither one is his, and they might be non-kosher meat. This story is the source for רב's rule that meat which went out of sight becomes forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: Cleaning or rinsing an animal's head
Meat that went out of sight, so we can no longer be sure it is the same kosher meat

steps.whyThisMatters: The rest of the סוגיא depends on this story, because רב's rule about unsupervised meat is learned from it.

phrases.english: [He was] cleaning a head; it fell from him.
phrases.notes: The story starts on the previous page. A man was rinsing an animal's head in the river.

phrases.english: He went and brought a basket,
threw it in, and brought up two.
phrases.notes: He lowered the basket into the river and pulled up two heads, not one.

phrases.english: Rav said: Do things really happen like this?
He forbade them to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story begun on the previous page as the source for רב's rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Meat that was out of sight and cannot be identified for sure is forbidden, so both heads were forbidden.

steps.title: Isn't permitted meat common too?
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא and רב אסי challenge רב: permitted meat is also common, so why assume the heads are forbidden?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא and רב אסי said to רב: Are forbidden pieces common and permitted ones not common?
steps.whatsHappening: Two students challenge רב's ruling. Kosher meat is around too, so why forbid the heads?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their point is that the found heads could just as easily be kosher. Without a reason to assume they are forbidden, it seems too strict to ban them.

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרִי לֵיהּ רַב כָּהֲנָא וְרַב אַסִּי לְרַב:
phrases.english: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi said to Rav:
Are forbidden ones common,
and permitted ones are not common?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי לֵיהּ רַב כָּהֲנָא וְרַב אַסִּי לְרַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's ruling in step 1.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Kosher meat is also common, so the found heads could be kosher. There is no reason to assume they are forbidden.

steps.title: רב answers: forbidden meat is more common here
steps.stepSummary: רב answers that in this place forbidden meat is more common, so the found heads are probably forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Forbidden ones are more common.
steps.whatsHappening: רב defends his ruling. Here, non-kosher meat is found more often than kosher meat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב agrees that kosher meat exists, but he says the majority in that place is non-kosher. So meat of unknown origin is more likely forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: Majority; we usually follow what is most common

phrases.english: He said to them: Forbidden ones are more common.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual answer: the majority in that place was forbidden
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Kosher and non-kosher meat are equally likely, so there is no reason to forbid.
steps.terutzMaskana: Forbidden meat is more common there, so the found heads are treated as forbidden.

steps.title: Why does it matter that the rule is only inferred?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if רב's rule is known only by inference from this story, what difference does that make?
steps.simpleTranslation: And if it is from an inference, what of it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why it matters that רב never said his rule outright and we only learn it from this story. This sets up the next answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the גמרא said that רב's rule about meat out of sight was learned only from a story. Now it asks what is wrong with learning a rule that way.

keyTerms.meaning: By inference; learned indirectly from a story, not said outright
What (here: what difference does it make?)

phrases.english: And if it is from an inference, what of it?
phrases.notes: This goes back to the point before the story: רב's rule is known only from this incident, not from his own direct words.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Steps back to ask how far the story can teach a general rule.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What weakness comes from knowing רב's rule only by inference from a story?

steps.title: It was a gentile port
steps.stepSummary: The answer: the story happened at a port of gentiles, where most meat was non-kosher, so it may not apply everywhere.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was a port of gentiles.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the story may not teach a general rule, because it happened in a place full of gentiles.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At a gentile port, most of the meat around is non-kosher. Maybe רב forbade the heads only for that reason. In a place where most meat is kosher, he might permit them.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't take the story as proof that רב forbids unsupervised meat everywhere. The גמרא is pointing out that the story may only apply to a place where most meat is non-kosher.

phrases.english: It was a port of gentiles,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The story took place at a gentile port, so it may only teach a rule for places where most meat is forbidden.

steps.title: Proof from רב's own answer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proves it was a gentile area: רב himself said 'forbidden meat is more common.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Know that this is so, for he said to them: 'Forbidden ones are more common.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings proof that the place was mostly non-kosher, using רב's own words from step 3.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's answer depended on forbidden meat being the majority there. That shows his ruling was tied to that place, not a rule for everywhere. The גמרא repeats his words here to make this new point.

keyTerms.meaning: Know (that this is so); introduces a supporting proof

steps.whatToRemember: The story teaches about a place where most meat was non-kosher. It does not clearly prove that רב forbids out-of-sight meat everywhere.

phrases.english: Know [that this is so], for he said to them:
"Forbidden ones are more common."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of step 5.
steps.raayaObject: That the story took place where most meat was forbidden

steps.title: How did רב ever eat meat?
steps.stepSummary: If רב forbids meat that went out of sight, how could he ever eat meat?
steps.simpleTranslation: But how did רב eat meat?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges: if meat becomes forbidden whenever it is out of sight, almost all meat would be forbidden. So how did רב eat meat at all?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Meat usually passes through other hands before it is eaten, like the butcher's or a messenger's. If every unwatched moment makes it forbidden, it seems impossible to eat meat. The answers follow in the next steps.

phrases.english: But Rav, how did he eat meat?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns to a practical difficulty with רב's strict rule.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's rule that meat out of sight is forbidden
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Meat is almost always out of someone's sight at some point, so this rule seems to make eating meat impossible.

steps.title: He ate it right away
steps.stepSummary: First answer: רב ate meat right after it was slaughtered, while it never left his sight.
steps.simpleTranslation: In its time, when he did not take his eyes off it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רב ate meat right away and kept watching it the whole time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the meat is watched from the slaughter until it is eaten, it is never 'out of sight.' So רב's rule never applied to it.

keyTerms.meaning: In its time; right away, soon after slaughter
Takes his eyes off it, stops watching it

phrases.english: In its time,
when he did not take his eyes off it.
phrases.notes: The word in round brackets is in the standard printed גמרא; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: First answer to the challenge in step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case: the meat was never out of sight
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב could never eat meat under his rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: He ate meat right away and watched it the whole time, so it never went out of sight.

steps.title: Meat that was tied and sealed
steps.stepSummary: Second answer: רב ate meat that was tied up and sealed, so no one could have switched it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you wish, say: he ate meat that was tied and sealed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another answer: the meat was wrapped and sealed, so even if no one watched it, it could not have been swapped.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry with out-of-sight meat is that it was exchanged for non-kosher meat. A seal shows no one tampered with it, so it counts as if it had been watched.

keyTerms.meaning: If you wish, say; introduces another possible answer

phrases.english: If you wish, say: [he ate meat that was] tied and sealed,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to step 7, besides the answer in step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternative answer: a seal protects the meat
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any meat that left his sight would be forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: Tied and sealed meat is safe from being switched, so it is permitted even though no one watched it.

steps.title: Meat with an identifying mark
steps.stepSummary: Third answer: רב ate meat that had a recognizable mark, like רבה בר רב הונא, who cut meat into three-cornered pieces.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or alternatively: by a mark, like רבה בר רב הונא, who would cut it into three-cornered pieces.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a third answer: the meat had a special sign, so רב could recognize it as his own. It gives רבה בר רב הונא's triangle cut as an example.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the meat has a unique mark, you can tell it is the same piece you had, even after it was out of sight. רבה בר רב הונא cut his meat into triangles for this reason.
steps.whatToRemember: Meat that left your sight is still allowed if: (1) it was really watched the whole time, (2) it was tied and sealed, or (3) it has an identifying mark.
steps.whyThisMatters: These three answers show what removes the worry of out-of-sight meat: supervision, a seal, or a recognizable sign.

phrases.english: Or alternatively: by a mark,

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הָא דְּרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא
phrases.english: like that [practice] of Rabba bar Rav Huna,
who would cut it into three-cornered pieces.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third answer to step 7, besides the answers in steps 8 and 9.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Meat that left his sight could never be trusted.
steps.terutzMaskana: Meat with a recognizable mark can be identified, so it stays permitted.

steps.title: רב sees the ferry arrive and takes it as a good sign
steps.stepSummary: On the way to his son-in-law רב חנן, רב sees the ferry coming right toward him and says this means a festive meal is waiting.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב was going to the house of רב חנן, his son-in-law. He saw the ferry coming toward him and said: 'The ferry is coming toward me, so a good day (a festive meal) must be waiting inside.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new story about רב that will connect to his strict rule about meat that left one's sight. This first part sets up the story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב treats the well-timed ferry as a hint that something good is waiting at his destination. This detail looks minor now, but the גמרא will come back to it later as a possible reason for רב's behavior.

keyTerms.meaning: A ferry, the boat that carries people across a river
Literally 'a good day'; here it means a festive meal

phrases.aramaic: רַב הֲוָה קָאָזֵיל לְבֵי רַב חָנָן חַתְנֵיהּ,
phrases.english: Rav was going to the house of Rav Chanan, his son-in-law.
He saw the ferry coming toward him.
He said: The ferry is coming toward me;
a good day is waiting inside.
phrases.notes: He means a festive meal is waiting for him at the house he is going to.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב הֲוָה קָאָזֵיל לְבֵי רַב חָנָן חַתְנֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After explaining how רב could ever eat meat, the גמרא brings a story that shows רב guarding meat in practice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Narrative setup: רב reads the timely ferry as a sign of a festive meal ahead.

steps.title: רב keeps his eyes on the meat, yet does not eat it
steps.stepSummary: At the house, רב sees hanging meat through a crack in the door. Everyone, even the butchers, comes out to greet him. רב keeps watching the meat and warns that unwatched meat could have been forbidden. Still, he does not eat it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He went and stood at the gate. He peeked through a crack in the door and saw an animal hanging. He knocked on the gate, and everyone came out to greet him, even the butchers. רב did not take his eyes off the meat. He told them: 'If you had relied on this now, you would have fed forbidden meat to my grandchildren.' And רב did not eat from that meat.
steps.whatsHappening: The story shows רב living by his rule: he never lets the meat out of his sight while everyone else leaves it. Then comes the surprise: he still refuses to eat it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since all the butchers left the meat, only רב's watching kept it from counting as 'out of sight.' His warning teaches that leaving meat alone even briefly can make it forbidden. His refusal to eat, even though he watched it, is a puzzle the גמרא will now try to solve.

keyTerms.meaning: He did not take his eyes off it, so it never left his sight

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רב refused the meat because it left anyone's sight. He made sure it never left HIS sight. That is exactly why the גמרא now asks what his reason was.

phrases.english: He went and stood at the gate.
He peeked through a crack in the door
and saw an animal hanging.
He knocked on the gate,
and everyone went out and came to greet him.
The butchers came out too.
Rav did not take his eyes off it (the meat).
He said to them: If you had relied on this now,
you would have fed forbidden food to my daughter's sons.
Rav did not eat from that meat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story from the ferry to the house.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Meat that everyone left unwatched would be forbidden. רב kept it in sight, but still did not eat it.

steps.title: Why did רב not eat? Not because it left his sight
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for רב's reason, and rules out the obvious one: the meat never left his sight.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? If you say it was because the meat was out of sight, that can't be, because it was not out of sight.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רב refused the meat and immediately rejects the most obvious answer. This prepares the next move, a different explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The usual reason to avoid meat in this סוגיא is that it 'went out of sight' (נתעלם מן העין). But the story stressed that רב never looked away, so that reason does not fit here. Some other reason must explain his refusal.

keyTerms.meaning: Being hidden or out of sight (like נִתְעַלֵּם מִן הָעַיִן)

phrases.english: What is the reason?
If it is because it was out of sight,
but it was not out of sight!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the puzzling end of the story in step 12.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רב refused meat that never left his sight.

steps.title: Suggested reason: רב had acted on a sign
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests רב held back because he had treated the ferry as a sign (נחוש), which is forbidden, so he punished himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it was because he had read a sign.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a new reason: רב was strict with himself because he had taken the ferry as an omen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Reading signs to predict good or bad (נחוש) is forbidden by the תורה. Since רב had said 'the ferry is coming, so a meal awaits,' he may have felt he did something wrong, and gave up the meal as a penalty. This ties the ferry detail from step 11 into the explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: He read a sign or omen (from נִחוּשׁ, a forbidden kind of fortune-telling)

phrases.english: Rather, it is because he read a sign.
phrases.notes: This points back to the ferry: רב read its arrival as a sign of a good meal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 13 with a new reason.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב refused the meat because he had relied on the ferry as an omen.

steps.title: Challenge: רב holds that this kind of sign is not real נחוש
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: רב himself taught that only a sign like those of אליעזר and יונתן, which they actually acted on, counts as נחוש.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't רב say: Any divination that is not like that of אליעזר, אברהם's servant, or like that of יונתן son of שאול, is not considered divination?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer of step 14 using רב's own teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אליעזר and יונתן actually made decisions based on their signs. רב only noticed the ferry and made a happy remark; he did not decide anything because of it. So by רב's own rule he did nothing forbidden, and there was no reason to punish himself.

keyTerms.meaning: A sign or omen that is forbidden to rely on
It is not considered forbidden omen-reading

phrases.english: But didn't Rav say:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל נַחַשׁ שֶׁאֵינוֹ כֶּאֱלִיעֶזֶר עֶבֶד אַבְרָהָם
phrases.english: Any divination that is not like that of Eliezer, the servant of Avraham,
phrases.notes: בראשית 24:14

phrases.english: or like that of Yonatan son of Shaul,
phrases.notes: שמואל א 14:8–12

phrases.english: is not divination!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָאָמַר רַב: כׇּל נַחַשׁ שֶׁאֵינוֹ כֶּאֱלִיעֶזֶר עֶבֶד אַבְרָהָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the answer of step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רב refused the meat because he had read a sign
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב's own rule says a sign is only forbidden if you act on it like אליעזר and יונתן did. רב's remark about the ferry did not qualify, so there was nothing to punish himself for.

steps.title: Final answer: it was an optional meal
steps.stepSummary: The real reason: it was a סעודת הרשות, an optional meal, and רב did not enjoy food at optional meals.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it was an optional meal, and רב did not take pleasure from an optional meal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the omen explanation and gives a new reason for רב's refusal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A meal for a מצוה (like a wedding or a ברית) is different from a meal held just for enjoyment. רב's personal practice was to avoid eating at meals that were not connected to a מצוה. So his refusal had nothing to do with the meat being forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: An optional meal, one not connected to a מצוה

steps.whatToRemember: רב guarded meat so it never left his sight, which shows how serious the rule of meat that went out of sight is. His refusal to eat in this story came from his personal practice of not enjoying optional meals, not from any problem with the meat.

phrases.english: Rather, it was an optional meal,
and Rav did not take pleasure from an optional meal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected answer of step 14 after the challenge in step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New explanation replacing the rejected one
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב refused the meat as a penalty for reading the ferry as a sign.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב refused because it was an optional meal, and he never enjoyed optional meals.

steps.title: Three sages and the signs they checked
steps.stepSummary: רב checked with a ferry, שמואל with a ספר, and רבי יוחנן with a child.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב would check with the ferry, שמואל would check with a book, and רבי יוחנן would check with a child.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the ferry came up in the last story, the גמרא now lists the kind of sign each of three great sages used to check what was ahead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This follows step 15, where רב taught that only a sign one actually acts on, like those of אליעזר and יונתן, is forbidden נחוש. Here we see that great sages did look at signs like these. The line also sets up the story about רבי יוחנן's child-sign that comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: would check, looking for a sign of what is ahead

phrases.english: Rav would check with the ferry,
phrases.notes: Like the story before: if the ferry came right away, he took it as a good sign.

phrases.english: and Shmuel would check with a book,
phrases.notes: He would open a ספר and look at the verse it opened to.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan would check with a child.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks up on the ferry mentioned in the previous discussion and widens it to other sages' signs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each of the three sages had his own way of checking for a sign: ferry, book, or child.

steps.title: Master for רב, colleague for שמואל
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן wrote to רב as 'our master in Bavel,' but after רב died he wrote to שמואל only as 'our colleague in Bavel.'
steps.simpleTranslation: All the years of רב, רבי יוחנן would write to him: 'To our master who is in בבל.' When רב died, he would write to שמואל: 'To our colleague who is in בבל.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story showing רבי יוחנן's child-sign in action. This step sets up the background: how רבי יוחנן addressed his letters.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The difference in titles shows that רבי יוחנן saw רב as his teacher but saw שמואל only as an equal. That gap is the problem that drives the rest of the story.

keyTerms.meaning: before, to (an opening greeting in a letter)
his soul rested, meaning he died

phrases.english: All the years of Rav,
Rabbi Yochanan would write to him
"To our master who is in Bavel."
When he died,
he would write to Shmuel
"To our colleague who is in Bavel."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a story that will show רבי יוחנן's way of checking a sign with a child.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יוחנן treated רב as his master but שמואל only as a colleague.

steps.title: שמואל sends the leap-year calculations
steps.stepSummary: שמואל, hurt, sent sixty years of leap-year calculations, but רבי יוחנן said this only shows he knows math.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: Does he not know any matter in which I am his teacher? He wrote and sent him the leap-year calculations for sixty years. רבי יוחנן said: Now he just knows math.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל tries to show רבי יוחנן that he deserves to be called a master, and sends him the leap-year calculations. רבי יוחנן is not impressed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל was famous for his knowledge of the calendar, so he chose that as proof. רבי יוחנן answers that skill with calculation does not make someone his teacher, so the title stays 'colleague.'

keyTerms.meaning: making a leap year (adding a month)

phrases.english: He said: Does he not know about me
phrases.notes: "He" here is שמואל, complaining about how רבי יוחנן addresses him.

phrases.english: any matter in which I am his teacher?
He wrote and sent him
the leap-year calculations for sixty years.
He said: Now, he just knows math.
phrases.notes: Now the speaker is רבי יוחנן, brushing off the calculations.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר: לָא יָדַע לִי מִידֵּי דְּרַבֵּיהּ אֲנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: שמואל responds to being called only a 'colleague.'
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Knowledge of calendar math alone did not make שמואל רבי יוחנן's master.

steps.title: Thirteen camels of טריפה questions and the child's verse
steps.stepSummary: שמואל sent thirteen camel-loads of ספקי טריפות. רבי יוחנן decided to visit his new master, but a child's verse 'ושמואל מת' made him think שמואל had died.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל wrote and sent him thirteen camel-loads of doubtful טריפה cases. רבי יוחנן said: I have a master in בבל; I will go see him. He said to a child: Recite your verse for me. The child said: 'And שמואל died.' רבי יוחנן said: Learn from this that שמואל has died.
steps.whatsHappening: This time שמואל's Torah knowledge wins over רבי יוחנן, who wants to travel to him. Before leaving, רבי יוחנן uses his child-sign, and the verse makes him conclude שמואל has died.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The huge collection of טריפה rulings is real Torah greatness, so רבי יוחנן now calls שמואל 'my master.' This is the child-sign from step 17 in action: רבי יוחנן reads the child's פסוק as a message about his trip.

keyTerms.meaning: recite your verse for me (the verse you learned)

phrases.english: He wrote and sent him
thirteen camel-loads of doubtful טריפה cases,
He said: I have a master in Bavel,
phrases.notes: Here רב means 'master' or 'teacher,' not the sage רב.

phrases.english: I will go see him.
He said to a child:
Recite your verse for me,
He said to him: "And Shmuel died,"
phrases.notes: שמואל א 28:3

phrases.english: He said: Learn from this
that Shmuel has died.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּתַב שַׁדַּר לֵיהּ תְּלֵיסַר גַּמְלֵי סְפֵקֵי טְרֵיפְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: שמואל's second attempt succeeds, and רבי יוחנן then checks his trip with a child's verse.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יוחנן accepted שמואל as his master, but the child's verse led him to conclude שמואל had died.

steps.title: שמואל had not really died
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the inference was wrong: שמואל was alive. The verse came only so רבי יוחנן would not trouble himself with the trip.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it was not so. שמואל had not died. Rather, it was so that רבי יוחנן would not trouble himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא steps in and corrects רבי יוחנן's conclusion: שמואל was still alive. The sign came out that way to save רבי יוחנן a hard journey.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן's 'שמע מינה' from the child's verse is rejected as a fact. The sign was real, but its purpose was to keep him from traveling, not to report that שמואל had died.
steps.whatToRemember: The three sages each used a sign: a ferry, a ספר, or a child's verse. In the story, the child's verse stopped רבי יוחנן's trip, even though שמואל had not really died.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the sign was false. The גמרא says it served a purpose: to spare רבי יוחנן the long trip.

phrases.english: But it was not so,
Shmuel had not died,
rather, it was so that
Rabbi Yochanan would not trouble himself.
phrases.notes: The trouble here is the long, hard trip from ארץ ישראל to בבל.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רבי יוחנן's conclusion from the child's verse in step 20.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the factual conclusion that שמואל had died; the sign itself still had a purpose.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רבי יוחנן read the verse as news of שמואל's death, when it was really meant to keep him from making the trip.

steps.title: A house, a child, and a wife can be a sign
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר teaches that a house, a child, or a wife is not forbidden ניחוש, but it can still be taken as a sign.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says: a house, a child, and a wife. Even though they are not ניחוש, they are a sign.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that continues the earlier stories about signs. It says some events in life can be treated as a 'sign' without being forbidden ניחוש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נחש means letting a random event decide what you will do, and that is forbidden. A סימן is different: you notice how things go after building a house, having a child, or marrying, and you take it as a good or bad sign. This is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: Forbidden divination: letting an omen decide your actions
A sign or indication (here, a permitted sign of good or bad fortune)
A house, a child, and a wife: major new beginnings in life

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up נחש and סימן. The ברייתא is not allowing ניחוש. It says these signs are a separate, permitted category.

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: It is taught in a ברייתא: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says:
A house, a child, and a wife –
phrases.notes: He means building a house, having a child, or marrying. How things go right afterward can be taken as a sign.

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין נַחַשׁ, יֵשׁ סִימָן.
phrases.english: even though they are not divination, they are a sign.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of signs from step 17 (the ferry, the ספר, the child), now through a ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A house, a child, or a wife may be taken as a sign, even though this is not forbidden ניחוש.

steps.title: A sign counts only after three times
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר limits the sign: it only counts once it has repeated three times. He brings a proof from יעקב's words about his sons.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: This applies only when the sign has been established three times, as it is written: 'יוסף is gone, and שמעון is gone, and you will take בנימין.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר adds a limit to the previous teaching. A sign is only reliable once it has happened three times in a row.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One event alone is not yet a sign. The proof comes from יעקב: losing יוסף and then שמעון was not yet a pattern, but losing בנימין would make three. That is why יעקב was so afraid to send him.

keyTerms.meaning: An established pattern, built through repetition

steps.whatToRemember: A sign is permitted (step 22), but it only counts once it repeats three times.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:
But this applies when it was established three times,
as it is written: 'Joseph is not,'
phrases.notes: בראשית 42:36

phrases.english: 'and Shimon is not,'
'and you will take Binyamin.'
phrases.notes: Losing בנימין would have made a third loss, and three makes a pattern.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: וְהוּא דְּאִיתַּחְזַק תְּלָתָא זִימְנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Qualifies the ברייתא in step 22 by limiting when a sign counts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A sign is reliable only after it has repeated three times, as shown by יעקב's words in בראשית 42:36.

steps.title: What about strung-together meat?
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא asks רב: if pieces of meat were strung together and went out of sight, does the string count as an identifying mark?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא asked רב: Meat on strings, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to its main topic: meat that was out of sight and may now be forbidden. רב הונא asks whether pieces tied together on a string count as an identifying mark.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Meat that disappears from view is normally forbidden, because we fear it was swapped for non-kosher meat. A סימן (identifying mark) lets you recognize it as the same meat. The question is whether the way pieces were strung together is a good enough mark.

keyTerms.meaning: Strung together, like beads on a string
Meat that went out of sight (the main topic of this part of the daf)

phrases.english: Rav Huna asked Rav:
With strung pieces, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב הוּנָא מֵרַב: בַּחֲרוּזִין מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the topic of signs and returns to the main topic of meat that went out of sight.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the way meat pieces were strung together count as an identifying mark that keeps the meat permitted?

steps.title: רב: obviously stringing is a mark
steps.stepSummary: רב answers sharply that of course strung meat counts as a סימן.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Do not be a fool. Strung pieces are an identifying mark.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers רב הונא's question. He treats the answer as so obvious that he scolds him for asking.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Calling the question foolish shows that רב saw no doubt here. The particular way the meat was strung is easy to recognize, so the meat can be identified and stays permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: Do not be a fool: the answer is obvious

phrases.english: He said to him: Do not be a fool;
strung pieces count as an identifying mark.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Strung meat is an obvious identifying mark, so it stays permitted.

steps.title: Second version: a plain ruling
steps.stepSummary: Another version says there was no question and answer. רב הונא simply reported רב's ruling that strung meat counts as a mark.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: רב הונא said in the name of רב: Strung pieces are an identifying mark.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of how this teaching was passed down. Here it is a plain statement, not an exchange.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The law is the same in both versions: stringing counts as a סימן. Only the form changes. In this version, רב הונא did not ask a question that got him scolded.
steps.whatToRemember: In both versions the law is the same: meat strung together has a סימן and stays permitted even after going out of sight.

phrases.english: There are those who say:
Rav Huna said that Rav said:
Strung pieces count as an identifying mark.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives another version of steps 24–25, with the same ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Strung meat counts as an identifying mark.

steps.title: Ravens drop meat on ערב יום כיפור
steps.stepSummary: Ravens drop livers and kidneys while רב נחמן is visiting רב כהנא. רב כהנא tells him to eat them, because on ערב יום כיפור kosher meat is far more common.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן of נהרדעא came to רב כהנא in פום נהרא on ערב יום כיפור. Ravens came and dropped livers and kidneys. He said to him: Take and eat. Today, permitted meat is more common.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story about meat that came from an unknown place. רב כהנא allows eating it because of what is common on that day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This meat has no סימן at all, and it was dropped by ravens. Still, it is permitted because most meat around on ערב יום כיפור comes from kosher slaughter, since everyone eats meat that day. So we follow the majority (רוב).

keyTerms.meaning: The day before יום כיפור (ערב יום כיפור)
Majority: following what is most common

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a ruling that meat with no סימן is always allowed. It is allowed here because kosher meat is so much more common on that specific day.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows a second way lost meat can be permitted: not through a סימן, but because most meat around at that time is kosher.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman of Neharde'a

phrases.aramaic: אִיקְּלַע לְגַבֵּי רַב כָּהֲנָא לְפוּם נַהֲרָא
phrases.english: happened to come to Rav Kahana in Pum Nahara
on the eve of Yom Kippur.
Ravens came and dropped livers and kidneys.
He said to him: Take and eat,
phrases.notes: רב כהנא, the host, is the one speaking to רב נחמן.

phrases.english: since today permitted meat is more common.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב נַחְמָן מִנְּהַרְדְּעָא אִיקְּלַע לְגַבֵּי רַב כָּהֲנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the topic of meat that went out of sight, now with a case where the meat is permitted by majority rather than by a סימן. It is the mirror image of steps 3 and 5: where forbidden meat is more common it is forbidden, and where permitted meat is more common, as on ערב יום כיפור, it is permitted.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Meat of unknown origin dropped by ravens on ערב יום כיפור may be eaten, because permitted meat is more common that day.

steps.title: רב הונא permits lost meat based on recognizing it by sight
steps.stepSummary: רב חייא בר אבין lost a piece of intestine meat among wine barrels. רב הונא permitted it because he recognized it by sight, even though it had no סימן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חייא בר אבין lost a piece of intestine meat among the wine barrels. He came before רב הונא. רב הונא asked: Do you have an identifying mark on it? He said: No. Do you recognize it by sight? He said: Yes. רב הונא said: If so, go take it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story. Meat went out of sight and had no identifying mark, but the owner recognized it by sight, and רב הונא allowed him to use it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now the סוגיא talked about a סימן as the way to identify meat that went out of sight. This story adds a second way: טביעות עין, recognizing the item by sight. The order of רב הונא's questions shows he checked for a סימן first, and when there was none, sight recognition was enough.

keyTerms.meaning: Recognizing something by sight; literally, the item is 'stamped' in your eye

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'בי דינא' does not mean a בית דין (court). It means the place where the wine barrels were kept.

phrases.english: Rav Chiyya bar Avin
lost a piece of intestine meat among the wine barrels,
phrases.notes: This isn't a court. דינא here means barrels, so he lost it in the wine cellar.

phrases.english: He came before Rav Huna.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִית לָךְ סִימָנָא בְּגַוֵּיהּ?
phrases.english: He said to him: Do you have an identifying mark on it?
He said to him: No.
Do you recognize it by sight?
He said to him: Yes.
If so, go take it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב חִיָּיא בַּר אָבִין אִיתְּבַד לֵיהּ כַּרְכְּשָׁא בֵּי דִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the stories about a סימן and about רוב, the גמרא now brings a case where there is no סימן but there is sight recognition.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Meat that went out of sight is permitted if the owner recognizes it by sight, even without a סימן.

steps.title: רב נחמן rules the same way about a lost side of meat
steps.stepSummary: רב חנינא חוזאה lost a side of meat. רב נחמן permitted it based on טביעות עין.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חנינא חוזאה lost a side of meat. He came before רב נחמן. רב נחמן asked: Do you have an identifying mark on it? He said: No. Do you recognize it by sight? He said: Yes. רב נחמן said: If so, go take it.
steps.whatsHappening: A second story follows the exact same pattern. This time the ruling comes from רב נחמן, about a large piece of meat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is that this was not one רב's private opinion. רב נחמן also relies on טביעות עין for meat that went out of sight. Repeating the case with a different authority makes the rule stronger.

keyTerms.meaning: A side (a large piece) of meat

phrases.english: Rav Chanina Chozaa
lost a side of meat,
He came before Rav Nachman.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִית לָךְ סִימָנָא בְּגַוֵּיהּ?
phrases.english: He said to him: Do you have an identifying mark on it?
He said to him: No.
Do you recognize it by sight?
He said to him: Yes.
If so, go take it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב חֲנִינָא חוֹזָאָה אִיתְּבַד לֵיהּ גַּבָּא דְּבִשְׂרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is a parallel story that backs up the ruling in step 28.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sight recognition is enough to permit meat that went out of sight.

steps.title: רב חסדא permits a lost bundle of תכלת wool by sight recognition
steps.stepSummary: רב נתן בר אביי lost a bundle of תכלת wool. רב חסדא let him use it based on טביעות עין.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נתן בר אביי lost a bundle of sky-blue wool. He came before רב חסדא. רב חסדא asked: Do you have an identifying mark on it? He said: No. Do you recognize it by sight? He said: Yes. רב חסדא said: If so, go take it.
steps.whatsHappening: A third story with the same pattern. This time the item is תכלת for ציצית, not meat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry with lost תכלת is that it may have been swapped for blue wool that is not kosher for ציצית. רב חסדא relies on sight recognition here too. This shows that טביעות עין works for more than just meat.

keyTerms.meaning: A bundle or skein of wool
תכלת, the sky-blue wool used for ציצית

steps.whatToRemember: Three different רבנן (רב הונא, רב נחמן, רב חסדא) all ruled that when there is no סימן, טביעות עין is enough to identify a lost item that went out of sight.

phrases.english: Rav Natan bar Abaye
lost a bundle of sky-blue wool,
He came before Rav Chisda.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִית לָךְ סִימָנָא בְּגַוֵּיהּ?
phrases.english: He said to him: Do you have an identifying mark on it?
He said to him: No.
Do you recognize it by sight?
He said to him: Yes.
If so, go take it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב נָתָן בַּר אַבָּיֵי אִיתְּבַד לֵיהּ קִיבּוּרָא דִּתְכֵלְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This third parallel story widens the rule from meat to תכלת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sight recognition is enough to identify lost תכלת as well.

steps.title: רבא begins: at first he thought a סימן was stronger than sight recognition
steps.stepSummary: רבא says his first assumption was that a סימן is better than טביעות עין, because lost items are returned to their owners based on a סימן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: At first I would say that an identifying mark is better than sight recognition, because we return a lost item based on an identifying mark,
steps.whatsHappening: רבא starts to share how his thinking changed. This line is a setup: he gives his first idea and its reason, and the rest of his thought comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's first reason is that the law of lost objects (אבידה) returns an item to someone who gives a סימן, so a סימן must be strong. The words 'at first I would say' tell us he is about to change his mind and explain why טביעות עין is actually stronger.

keyTerms.meaning: At first I would say (an opinion he later dropped)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not take this as רבא's final view. 'מרישא הוה אמינא' means 'at first I thought,' so a change of mind is coming.

phrases.english: Rava said:
At first I would say
that an identifying mark is better than sight recognition,
since we return a lost item based on an identifying mark,

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: מֵרֵישָׁא הֲוָה אָמֵינָא סִימָנָא עֲדִיף מִטְּבִיעוּת עֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the three stories rely on טביעות עין, רבא starts to compare how strong a סימן is against טביעות עין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבא's first assumption, which he will revise: a סימן is stronger than טביעות עין, since lost items are returned by a סימן.
